articles.title: Paper Unicorns Are Cheap. Building A $1B Revenue AI Company Takes A Multimarket Cap Table
articles.snippet: AI startups should be judged by durable revenue, full-price renewals and healthy margins after delivery costs, with embedded customer workflows providing stronger defensibility as model access gets cheaper, rather than their paper valuation, writes guest author Ilman Shazhaev, founder and CEO of Dizzaract, who suggests that founders should build global investor bases that support customer acquisition and market entry while weighing venture growth expectations against sovereign-backed investors’ localization, governance and other obligations.
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence • SaaS • Sales & Marketing • Venture
Paper Unicorns Are Cheap. Building A $1B Revenue AI Company Takes A Multimarket Cap Table
Guest Author
November 9, 2026
Guest Author
0
Shares

By Ilman Shazhaev
A $1 billion valuation still makes a startup a unicorn on paper. Yet when 250 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in the first half of 2026, the speed of wealth creation raised another question : How many of these businesses can keep their customers once the initial excitement fades?
I would set a higher benchmark for unicorns with $1 billion in revenue sustained by customers who keep paying.
I spent five years at Harbin Institute of Technology and Shanghai Jiao Tong University , where “fail fast, improve faster” shaped my approach to building technology. Having studied in China before building an AI company in Abu Dhabi, I have also seen how the same growth story can raise different questions among investors, eventually boiling down to: “What will customers keep paying for?”
The revenue test investors should demand
Ilman Shazhaev, founder and CEO of Dizzaract.
Fast revenue deserves attention. Founders who turn pilots into paying deployments are solving a real problem, and strong sales can make the next round easier. An annualized run rate built from discounts, experimental budgets or generous compute subsidies, however, offers little assurance that customers will stay.
Since 2023, the price of hitting a fixed level of AI performance has dropped thirteenfold every year. Startups that just resell model access now face brutal price competition. Look at OpenRouter and its $113 million Series B: developers can already swap between models through one shared interface.
Businesses built around proprietary workflows face a different test. Software embedded in a company’s approvals, records and daily decisions can be far harder to replace than the model doing the underlying work. I would check whether customers renew at full price and expand their contracts. Then I would see whether margins stay healthy after inference costs.
Why the cap table should cross borders
Once founders know who keeps buying, they should raise across regions, because a local backer can double as market entry. Borders barely slow an AI product down. Enterprise sales still depend on local budgets, procurement procedures and relationships. A foreign investor becomes valuable when those connections turn a product demonstration into a paid contract.
The $30 million Series A for London- and Gulf-based 1001 AI offers a useful example . U.S. venture firm Lux Capital led the financing, alongside Saudi PIF-backed Sanabil Investments . The deal cannot establish future retention by itself, but it shows how capital, talent and customers can sit on different maps, with engineers in London and customers in the Gulf.
Ask every investor what they bring besides money. One warm introduction to the right buyer can beat a higher valuation if it turns into a contract you can actually deliver and renew.
Different money, different obligations
The choice between traditional venture funding and sovereign-backed money is often framed as a choice between fast and patient capital. I find the more practical distinction lies in the obligations attached to each check.

articles.title: Nominal Secures $240 Million in Lightspeed-Led Financing at $3 Billion Valuation
articles.snippet: Nominal Secures $240 Million in Lightspeed-Led Financing at $3 Billion Valuation Securities.io
articles.text:
Funding
Nominal Secures $240 Million in Lightspeed-Led Financing at $3 Billion Valuation
Published
November 9, 2026
By
Hana Mori Enterprise Data & AI Platforms, AI Research Agent
Add Securities.io to your preferred sources on Google
Table Of Contents
Nominal announced on November 9, 2026 that it had raised $240 million at a $3 billion valuation, in a financing led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners. The financing is intended to give hardware engineering teams a platform on which they can build.
The valuation is three times the $1 billion valuation Nominal disclosed on March 5, 2026, calculated from the two announced figures. That earlier financing brought an additional $80 million and was led by Founders Fund, with continued support from Sequoia, General Catalyst, Lux Capital, Red Glass and Lightspeed.
From Test Data to Engineering Applications
Nominal describes its platform as a system built around the data produced by physical hardware. It ingests telemetry, video, logs and files from test stands, vehicles and other tools, keeping each run’s channels and metadata together. Data sources can be synchronized on a single timeline, while search, streaming monitors, data-driven procedures, cross-run trending and reports connect day-to-day analysis to the underlying engineering record.
Nominal’s Analyst agent searches engineering data, compares runs and shows the steps behind its answers. APIs, software-development kits and MCP connections let customers build their own applications and agents. The platform can run in Nominal’s cloud, a customer’s virtual private cloud, on premises or fully offline, covering both connected development environments and disconnected field sites.
In its March announcement, Nominal reported that more than 60 organizations used its software, revenue had grown sevenfold during the preceding 10 months and its team had more than tripled to 135 people.
A May 21, 2026 profile by Sequoia Capital subsequently described 75 global customers across aerospace, defense, energy and transportation. That provides a later marker of adoption between the two financings, although the customer figures come from different company and investor disclosures.
Expansion Through Acquisitions and Government Work
Nominal said in March that its expansion plan included strategic acquisitions in the United States and Europe and a move beyond aerospace and defense into automotive, energy, manufacturing and robotics.
On November 6, 2026, Nominal acquired Pull Systems , whose Workbench telemetry platform was developed with Porsche and other Volkswagen Group brands. It serves field-monitoring, quality and service teams investigating new vehicle programs. Nominal said those teams could use Workbench to identify root causes in minutes rather than months. Pull Systems co-founder Henry joined work on Nominal for Developers, while co-founder Manny is helping develop Analyst.
A separate funding disclosure came on October 26, 2026, when Nominal announced its selection for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase package under the competitive AFWERX program. That package consists of $30 million of private matching and $41.2 million of government funding across Air Force and Navy programs. It supports the capture, organization, analysis and sharing of aircraft test and telemetry data for Collaborative Combat Aircraft development and other work involving AFWERX, the Air Force Test Pilot School and the Navy Program Executive Office

articles.title: Space Startups 2026: 6 Companies That Raised $200M+ Rounds
articles.snippet: Space Startups 2026: 6 Companies That Raised $200M+ Rounds AI Funding Tracker
articles.text:
Space startups raised a record amount of private capital in the third quarter of 2026. Seraphim Space counted $20.8 billion invested in Q3, more than two and a half times the prior quarterly high of $8.0 billion set in Q1.
This list covers six companies that closed priced rounds of $200 million or more between June and September 2026. Each round was announced by the company or reported by a named outlet. The companies are grouped by where they sit in the space supply chain.
Startup Supply-chain layer Latest round Milestone tied to the round
Stoke Space Launch $1B Series E, Sep 2026 First orbital Nova launch targeted for early 2027
The Exploration Company Cargo transport and return $450M Series C, Sep 2026 ESA service contract for Nyx, Sep 2026
K2 Space Satellite manufacturing $500M Series D at $6.8B, Jul 2026 Gravitas spacecraft launched March 2026
Varda Space Industries In-orbit manufacturing $251M Series D at $1.6B, Sep 2026 Six reentry missions completed
ICEYE Radar imaging €450M primary Series F at over €10B, Jun 2026 Systems supplied to seven European governments
Hubble Network Satellite connectivity $200M Series C at $1.6B, Sep 2026 Network opened to all Bluetooth LE devices
Launch capacity set the pace for 2026 space funding
Space Capital described Q3 2026 as the quarter the space economy ran out of launch capacity. The firm tracked $22.2 billion invested across 132 companies in the quarter and $92.5 billion through the first nine months of the year.
That nine-month total already beat 2025’s full-year record of $55.3 billion. Space Capital counts a wider set of deals than Seraphim, so the two trackers report different totals for the same period.
Capital is also concentrated. The top 10 rounds took 78% of all money deployed in Q3, up from 57% in Q2, according to Seraphim.
The quarter’s largest deals were Blue Origin’s $10 billion late-stage raise, Hadrian’s $1.37 billion Series D, and Stoke Space’s $1 billion Series E. Blue Origin took outside capital for the first time in 26 years.
Space sits alongside other frontier sectors, such as autonomous systems and physical AI, that EmergeFolio follows as emerging technology areas.
Space startups building transport to orbit and back
Stoke Space
Stoke Space is building Nova, a rocket designed to be fully and rapidly reusable. The Kent, Washington company completed an initial close of a $1 billion Series E on September 8, 2026, co-led by Point72 Ventures and Spark Capital.
The round brought total capital raised to $2.3 billion since its 2020 founding. Stoke did not publish a valuation, though a person familiar with the deal put it at roughly $10 billion. Nova has not yet reached orbit, and Stoke is targeting its first orbital launch in early 2027.
The Exploration Company
The Exploration Company raised $450 million (about €387 million) in a Series C announced on September 8, 2026. Bessemer Venture Partners, Atomico, and the EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund co-led the round. The company called it the largest Series C ever raised by a European space company.
The money funds Nyx, a reusable capsule for cargo to and from low Earth orbit, and Storm, a reusable rocket engine. Two days later, the European Space Agency signed a service contract for Nyx under its ALADDIN cargo capsule project. Total funding stands at about $680 million.
